profile.summary: 1 Kings presents the height and fall of the united kingdom of Israel, beginning in the last days of David, passing through the splendour of Solomon's reign, and coming to the division of the kingdom after his death. The book contrasts wisdom, wealth and national greatness with the spiritual fragility of a people who departs from fidelity to the Lord. The narrative shows that political prosperity does not replace the obedience of the covenant, and that God continues to speak through prophets to confront kings and call his people back to Him.
profile.setting: The main historical scene is the monarchical period of Israel, from the end of David's reign to about 853 BC, encompassing the reign of Solomon, the division of the kingdom, and the early years of Israel and Judah as two distinct kingdoms. The international context favored Israel's expansion in Solomon's time, as traditional powers such as Hittites, Assyria and Egypt were weakened to varying degrees. After the division, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah lived constant political pressure from neighbors such as Egypt, Aram, and Assyria, while internally faced instability, dynastic rivalry, and spiritual decline. As for authorship and composition, the introduction presents 1-2 Kings as the work of a single anonymous author, possibly identified by the Jewish tradition with Jeremiah, but this is uncertain; the date of writing is subsequent to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

structure.label: Transition from David to Solomon
structure.description: Last days of David, disputes for the succession and initial consolidation of Solomon's throne.

structure.label: The peak and the fall of Solomon
structure.description: Request for wisdom, prosperity, construction of the temple and palace, international fame and subsequent spiritual infidelity that prepares the division of the kingdom.

structure.label: Division of the kingdom and deterioration of the two monarchies
structure.description: Reaction of Rehoboam, separation between Israel and Judah, political instability in the north and progressive spiritual degradation in the two kingdoms.

structure.label: The prophetic ministry of Elijah
structure.description: Confrontation with the worship of Baal, demonstration of the exclusive power of the Lord, escape from Elijah and his re-reception, with the indication of his successor.

structure.label: The campaigns of Ahab and the closing of the book
structure.description: Conflicts of Ahab over the Arameans, the episode of Naboth, the word of the prophets, and the conclusion with mentions to Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah.

themes: Loyalty to the covenant as the evaluation of kings
The dangers of prosperity, luxury and spiritual self-confidence
God's sovereignty over the politics and history of nations
The central role of the prophets in the correction and warning of the people
The Consequences of Spiritual Infidelity for Leaders and Nation
readingKeys: Notice how each king is evaluated less for his political success and more for his fidelity to the Lord.
Pay attention to the three apparitions of God to Solomon and how they mark promise, warning, and judgment.
Read the accounts of the prophets as the interpretive axis of the book: they explain the spiritual meaning of events.
profile.cautions: The introduction highlights Solomon's greatness, but makes sure to show that external brightness does not guarantee spiritual fidelity. It is also important to remember that the traditional authorship attributed to Jeremiah is not certain, and that the chronology of kings involves overlaps and co-regences, which makes some dates approximate. The book is not just a political narrative: its main focus is theological, evaluating kings and people by the relationship with the covenant with God.

dossier.narratedEra: 1 Kings tells of the final period of David, the reign of Solomon, and the initial history of the monarchy divided into Israel and Judah. According to the notes, the narrative arc begins with David's last days and follows the government of Solomon (approx. 971-931 BC), passing through the rupture after his death in 931 BC, and accompanies the two kingdoms until about 853 BC, in the time of Jehoshaphat in Judah and Ahaziah in Israel. The setting includes the expansion of the Solomonic kingdom in the middle of the 10th century BC, contacts with Tyre and Egypt, the political division between the north and south, and the increased external pressure of Aram and Assyria throughout the 9th century BC.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes describe 1 to 2 Kings as the work of a single unknown author, with a coherent perspective; the Jewish tradition identifies him with Jeremiah. This author would have used official archives of the palace and temple and prophetic records, composing the work after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. There is also the possibility of a final appendix added after the liberation of Joaquim in 561/562 BC, if the main author has not lived until then. Thus, the date of composition is post-586 BC, but this should not be confused with the narrated time, which is much earlier.

politics.title: Succession of David: Adonijah tries to usurp the throne
politics.detail: In 1 Kings 1, Adonijah says, "I will make myself king," supported by Joab and Abiathar, while Solomon is confirmed by David, Nathan, Zadok, and Benaiah. The note highlights that Solomon was the legitimate heir chosen by God, and that the dispute already anticipates later conflicts at the end of Solomon's reign and after the division of the kingdom.
politics.readingImpact: The scene is not just a family crisis; it establishes the theme of dynastic legitimacy and shows that succession in Israel had political and theological weight.

politics.title: Salomonic Empire and Administrative Expansion
politics.detail: At the height, Solomon ruled a kingdom that extended to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. The notes describe government reorganization, commercial expansion by land and sea, and great works, such as the temple and the palatial complex. The external context favored this expansion because the traditional powers were weakened: fragmented hithes, still weak Assyria and Egypt in retraction in Canaan.
politics.readingImpact: Solomon's splendour helps to explain why the book celebrates its greatness, but also why his politics and wealth extend the danger of spiritual infidelity.

politics.title: Division of the kingdom after Solomon's death
politics.detail: With the death of Solomon in 931 BC, the tension between northern and southern tribes comes to the fore. Rehoboram rejects the request for relief for forced labor and heavy taxes, and the northern tribes separate, forming Israel with Jeroboam I; Judah remains under Reoboam. The note also notes that hostility between the two kingdoms continued for generations, with intervals of temporary cooperation.
politics.readingImpact: The division is read as an immediate historical judgment on Solomon's infidelity, and not as a simple administrative dispute.

politics.title: International pressures in time of Ahab and Jeosafá
politics.detail: In the reign of Ahab, the political scene is shaped by the Western expansion of Assyria under Salmaneser III and the rivalry with Aran. The note links the three-year truce without war to the Assyrian threat and the confrontation of Qarqar (853 BC), where a Western coalition, including Ahab, resisted the Assyrian advance. The alliance of family ties between Ahab and Jehoshaphat also appears through Atalia's marriage to Jehoram.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the local wars of 1 Rs 20-22 are inserted in a larger international board, which gives strategic weight to the decisions of the kings.

politics.title: Jeroboam and the institutionalization of the religious rupture in the north
politics.detail: Jeroboam I is presented as the first king of the northern kingdom and as someone who diverted Israel through apostate religious practices. The notes link their policy to the spiritual collapse of the north and to the model that would last until the exile of the kingdom, mentioned in another later passage cited by the introduction.
politics.readingImpact: The political split is not neutral: the new regime is born already marked by an unfaithful cultical reform, which affects the reading of the rest of the northern history.

politics.title: Ahab, Ben-Hadade and the struggle with the Arameans
politics.detail: The end of the book emphasizes three campaigns of Ahab against the Aramean king Ben-hadad. The last battle cost Ahab's life; before that, the tension between Israel and Aram reappears repeatedly, with prophets warning and censoring the king. The note also mentions Naboth's execution and the appropriation of his vineyard, an act that deepens the moral crisis of the kingdom.
politics.readingImpact: Ahab's foreign policy appears inseparable from his internal corruption; the book unites war, injustice, and prophetic judgment.

customs.title: Diplomatic weddings between royal houses
customs.detail: The notes say that marriage alliances with daughters of foreign kings were a common practice in the Ancient Near East to seal agreements. In 1 Rs 11, however, this custom becomes spiritually disastrous for Solomon, because his foreign wives turn their hearts away from other gods.
customs.readingImpact: The custom helps to understand the diplomatic logic of the time without softening the negative evaluation of the biblical text about its spiritual consequences.

customs.title: Joint Regency to Ensure Ordered Succession
customs.detail: The note of 1 KR 1:35 explains that co-regency was common in Israel and Egypt. Solomon would have exercised public office for about two years before David's death, which facilitated the transition of power. The same phenomenon reappears in the divided monarchy.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands why dates of reign can overlap and why biblical chronology is not always strictly linear.

customs.title: Anointing, real procession and signs of legitimacy
customs.detail: Solomon's anointing by Zadok and Nathan follows a known protocol in the ancient world. Assembling the king's mule was a sign of prestige and public authorization; the procession at Gihom made David's approval visible. The anointing with oil also conferred divine sanction on the ceremony.
customs.readingImpact: These gestures show that the royal legitimacy was public, ritual and theological, not just political.

customs.title: Ritual refuge in the altar and the logic of clemency
customs.detail: Adonijah seeks the "points of the altar" in 1 Rs 1:50-53, a gesture that the notes relate to the biblical precedent for involuntary murder. As his action was treason, the protection did not come automatically; only the king could grant forgiveness. The text thus illuminates the use of sacred space as a place of legal appeal.
customs.readingImpact: The scene shows how worship and justice crossed; the altar did not serve as an automatic escape, but as a request for mercy within the covenant order.

customs.title: Economy, forced labor and popular claim
customs.detail: The division of the kingdom is linked to the request of the people for relief from forced labour and heavy taxes. The notes indicate that Solomon's administrative policy became oppressive and contributed to the northern rebellion.
customs.readingImpact: The problem is not only ideological; there is real economic and social strain behind the political collapse.

customs.title: Cult, ritual prostitution and pagan practices
customs.detail: The notes note that Jehoshaphat's reforms had not yet removed all pagan sanctuaries and that there were cult prostitutes associated with these centers. In 1 Rs 11, foreign cults and sacrifice of children linked to Molekh, denounced as detestable.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of the book gains density: the crisis of Israel includes concrete religious practices, not just theological abstraction.

language.title: "Monbtures as an image of david continuity
language.detail: In 1 Rs 11:36, the note states that the "lamp" represents the descendants of David as living bearers of the promises of the covenant, with later Messianic resonance.
language.readingImpact: The image guides the reading of the kingdom of Judah as a sign of permanence of the divine promise despite Solomon's failure.

language.title: Tear the cloak in twelve parts as a symbolic act
language.detail: Ahias tears his robe into twelve pieces and delivers ten to Jeroboam. The notes treat this as a symbolic prophetic act that dramatizes the future division of tribes.
language.readingImpact: The gesture transforms a political decision into a visible sign of God's judgment, linking narrative and prophecy.

language.title: Image of the shepherd and sheep
language.detail: In 1 Rs 22:17, the note highlights that kings and leaders were seen as pastors of the people. The metaphor is applied to Ahab, but it also prepares a later messianic reading of the Good Shepherd.
language.readingImpact: The image gives moral criterion to judge rulers: leadership is cared for, not self-preservation.

language.title: Hebrew nuance in 1 Rs 22:15
language.detail: The note notes that the word "sarsatically" does not appear in Hebrew; the translation only explains the tone perceived by Ahab. This shows an interpretative decision of the version, not a word of the original text.
language.readingImpact: The reader is reminded that some speech tones are inferred by the translator to make explicit the irony of dialogue.

language.title: The term for "governing" and its theological weight
language.detail: In 1 Rs 1:35, the notes indicate that the Hebrew term ruler for theorator may have theological scope, because the king is seen simultaneously as the administrative and spiritual leader of the people of God.
language.readingImpact: The vocabulary of government in 1 Kings is not merely civil; it carries responsibility for alliance.

timeline.title: Last days of David and the beginning of the succession
timeline.detail: The opening of the book places the reader in the last years of David, when his physical weakness triggers the dispute between Adonijah and Solomon. The notes associate this at the end of a phase of war and wear and tear of the king.
timeline.readingImpact: The beginning of the book links dynastic transition to human fragility, preparing the emphasis on God's fidelity to the Davidic covenant.

timeline.title: Reign of Solomon: about 971-931 BC
timeline.detail: The notes date the reign of Solomon from 971 to 931 BC. It represents the height of Israel's glory, followed by a progressive spiritual and political fall.
timeline.readingImpact: This chronological frame helps you read 1 Kings 1-11 as the rise, peak and decline in the same generation.

timeline.title: Division of the kingdom in 931 BC.
timeline.detail: Solomon's death in 931 BC marks the formal separation between Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Reoboam and Jeroboam become the initial poles of this new reality.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology reinforces that the division is a decisive and structuring event for all the rest of the book.

timeline.title: Invasion of Sisaak and the vulnerability of Judah
timeline.detail: The notes place the invasion of Sisakh (Shishak) around 926 BC, already in the reign of Rehobone. This shows that the internal rupture left the realms exposed to external aggressions.
timeline.readingImpact: The spiritual fall has immediate geopolitical consequences; newly-fragmented independence is already under foreign pressure.

timeline.title: Battle of Qarqar and the year 853 BC
timeline.detail: The note links 1 Rs 22 to the confrontation of Qarqar in 853 BC, when a Western coalition, including Ahab, faced Salmaneser III. The episode marks the international backdrop of the end of 1 Kings.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps the reader to place Ahab's death in a broad, unused historical context.

timeline.title: Closure in Ahaziah of Israel and transition to 2 Kings
timeline.detail: The book ends with the reign of Ahaziah in Israel, about 853-852 BC, and prepares the continuation of 2 Kings.
timeline.readingImpact: The end does not complete the entire history of the monarchy, but closes a critical stage of the division and opens another.

investigation: The tradition of Jeremian authorship appears in the notes, but remains as a traditional identification, not as independent evidence.
The dates of reign are presented as approximate and, in some cases, complex because of co-regensions; the note itself admits chronological difficulties.
The coverage of the notes is selective: Solomon privileges, the division of the kingdom, Eliah/Ahab and Jehoshaphat, leaving other kings only summarized.
Some archaeological and historical details are cited as illustrative support, but remain dependent on the secondary source provided, not external demonstration here.

The confessional readings of the notes repeatedly connect the story of 1 Kings to the Davidic promise and messianic expectation; this dossier preserves this perspective without widening it beyond what the source states.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes and therefore does not intend to be exhaustive. There are real gaps: many passages from 1 Kings do not receive historical-cultural commentary in the sources, and various elements are summarized rather than detailed. Tyndale's notes focus mainly on royal succession, international alliances, worship and prophets; Matthew Henry offers a panoramic and devotional view, but few specific historical data. There are also controversies recognized by the source itself, especially in the chronologies of the kings and at the final date of composition. When the note suggests tradition or inference, this was marked as an interpretation or question debated, without turning hypothesis into a proven fact.
